speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: As the Bill amendments are market-sensitive, this approach brings the Bill into effect the day after its introduction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Before I go through the key amendments in the Bill, let me explain the rationale for the changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Today, residential properties can be acquired directly or via equity interests, including unlisted shares, in Property Holding Entities, or PHEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These refer to entities whose primary tangible assets are residential properties in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Direct acquisitions of residential property are subject to Buyer's Stamp Duty, or BSD, and, where applicable, Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty or ABSD.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Acquisitions of unlisted shares in PHEs are subject to share duty of 0.2%, based on the purchase price or the value of the shares.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Such acquisitions may also be subject to ACD, if the acquirer is a significant owner of the PHE or becomes one after the acquisition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: A significant owner is a person who beneficially owns at least 50% of the equity interests or voting power in the PHE.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: ACD was introduced in 2017 to address the stamp duty rate differential that previously existed between the direct acquisition or disposal of residential properties and the acquisition or disposal of equity interests in PHEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: ABSD and ACD thus operate together to promote a stable and sustainable residential property market in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: ACD (Trust) follows from the introduction of ABSD (Trust).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: With ACD (Trust), ACD may apply when equity interests in a PHE are transferred into a living trust, regardless of whether there is an identifiable beneficial owner of those interests at the time of transfer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These changes ensure similar stamp duty treatment for transfers of residential property or equity interests in a PHE, whether acquired directly or through a trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: If an Institution of a Public Character, or IPC, is the sole beneficial owner of the residential property or equity interests in a PHE transferred into the trust, among other conditions, the IPC can apply for a remission of ABSD (Trust) or ACD (Trust).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Today, donations of immovable property or unlisted shares to IPCs qualify for stamp duty remission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: To determine whether ACD (Trust) applies to the acquisition of equity interests in a PHE that are to be held on a trust for beneficiaries who are not identifiable beneficial owners, we will consider the equity interests in the PHE that are to be held by the trustee of the trust for those beneficiaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This consideration is only of the portion of interests to be held on trust for those beneficiaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For example, if the trustee is to hold 10% equity interests in a PHE for identifiable beneficial owners and another 5% for other beneficiaries who are not identifiable beneficial owners, only the 5% equity interests will be considered to be held by the trustee for the purpose of determining whether ACD (Trust) applies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: ACD (Trust) will apply in such a case only if the trustee is a significant owner with at least 50% equity interests or voting power in the PHE or becomes one after the acquisition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In determining the trustee's significant ownership status, the equity interests that are beneficially owned by the trustee's associates will be treated as beneficially owned by the trustee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: A treatment for associates already exists in the ACD regime to cover arrangements under which individual buyers act in concert to purchase equity interests, with the objective of avoiding ACD.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Examples of associates include parents, children, spouses and associated companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In assessing whether an identifiable beneficial owner of equity interests in a PHE is a significant owner of the PHE, the interests beneficially owned by the beneficial owner and the beneficial owner's associates will be considered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In the instance where a trustee holds equity interests for a beneficiary who is not an identifiable beneficial owner of those interests at the time of their transfer into the trust, such a beneficiary is considered an associate of the trustee in determining whether the trustee is a significant owner of the PHE.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This definition of associates will be provided for in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: ACD (Trust) may also apply if the trustee, being a significant owner of a PHE, disposes of the trustee's equity interests that were held on trust for a beneficiary who is not an identifiable beneficial owner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: If the trustee disposes of the equity interests within three years after acquiring them, the trustee will be liable to pay ACD at the prevailing ACD rate of 12% for sellers, equivalent to the highest Seller's Stamp Duty, or SSD, rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In addition, where the trustee transfers equity interests to a beneficiary of the trust who was not an identifiable beneficial owner of those interests at the time they were transferred into the trust, the beneficiary will be liable to pay the prevailing ACD for buyers if the beneficiary is a significant owner or becomes one after the transfer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill provides for this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Next, clause 4 of the Bill introduces a new section 22C which imposes a statutory duty on the original beneficial owner of a trust residential property who renounces his or her interest in the property, such that this interest reverts to the settlor of the trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The original beneficial owner is one who beneficially owns the property at the time it is transferred into the trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The original beneficial owner must give a written notice of the renunciation to the settlor and to the Commissioner of Stamp Duties within a specified period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: If he or she fails to do so, and the Commissioner becomes aware of this, for example, through IRAS' regular audit, the Commissioner may give the notice to the original beneficial owner and the settlor instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The notice, whether given by the original beneficial owner or the Commissioner, will be chargeable with stamp duty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Specifically, the settlor will be liable to pay BSD and, where applicable, ABSD.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This treatment for the renunciation of interest by an original beneficial owner will ensure that where the beneficial ownership of a trust residential property reverts to the settlor, the settlor would have to pay stamp duty, similar to if he or she had acquired the property directly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 8 and 9 make transitional provisions to modify the application of the Bill to matters occurring between 10 May 2022 and the date the amending Act is published in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two short clarifications to raise on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, in determining whether a grantee or grantor is a significant owner of a property holding entity, the new section 23 will take into account equity interests held by an associate of the grantor or grantee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IRAS has provided on its website guidance on who is to be deemed an associate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes parties with an agreement or arrangement, whether oral, written, expressed, implied, to act together to acquire, hold or dispose of equity interest in, or to exercise votes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Determining the existence of an oral or implied agreement or arrangement is a very fact-specific exercise that can be very time- and resource-consuming.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does not seem practical for IRAS to be undertaking such an assessment for every transaction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify under what circumstances will IRAS undertake the process to determine the existence of any oral or implied agreement or arrangement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, my clarification has to do with the related changes to the ABSD regime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There may be a case of a discretionary trust with no identifiable beneficial trust that was set up before 9 May 2022 where action was subsequently taken after 9 May 2022 to appoint assets to an identifiable beneficiary or to distribute assets to any identifiable beneficiary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify if the documents which arise after 9 May 2022 for such a trust is stampable under the new ABSD (Trust) regime?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Most adult Singaporeans would have encountered, or rather, paid stamp duties at various points in their life, most commonly, when buying property.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, indeed, stamp duty is a tax on dutiable documents relating to any immovable property in Singapore and any stock or shares.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These include the sale and purchase of property, lease or rental of property, mortgage of property and shares and shares transfers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond a revenue collection tool, stamp duty has also evolved to play a significant role as a macro-prudential tool to address risks in the property sector, especially in the past decade or so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is the case not just in Singapore, but also in other jurisdictions, such as Hong Kong and Australia, as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From a simple Buyer's Stamp Duty, or BSD, this has now evolved to include Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty, or ABSD, and Seller's Stamp Duty, or SSD, for certain classes of property, such as residential and industrial properties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The differentiated rates of stamp duty have also been adjusted ever so frequently, most recently, in the December 2021 round of cooling measures where Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs) buying their second and subsequent property and all foreigners and entities saw raised ABSD rates of 5% to 15%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nonetheless, as a tax that is levied on the market values of leases, properties and shares, stamp duty receipts are affected by the stage of the market cycle and, more importantly, should grow over time, in tandem with inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From around $1.26 billion in FY2000, stamp duty receipts have grown to $3.28 billion in FY2010 and $3.9 billion in FY2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is most impressive about this revenue source is that this growth over the past decade or so is despite the smaller Government Land Sales programme and a lower level of property market transactions today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For FY2022, stamp duty receipts are expected to remain robust at $5.24 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, I have also observed that actual operating revenue collections for FY2021 have turned out to be higher, as compared to what was initially budgeted for in Budget 2021 and even the revised estimate as of Budget 2022 announced earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would already be more than sufficient to cover the $1.5 billion support package announced on 21 June.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I do agree with the Government that there need not be a further draw from the reserves, as the package can simply be funded from the better-than-expected fiscal outturn in FY2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, it also appears that while FY2021 operating revenues are higher by about $2.1 billion compared to the revised estimate presented earlier this year, both operating and development expenditures are lower by a combined $3.6 billion, which, I understand, is due to lower-than-budgeted spending on COVID-19 response measures as the Omicron variant turned out less severe than expected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Combining higher revenues and lower expenses would mean that the Government's primary deficit improved by $5.7 billion, which, again, is more than sufficient to cover the recent $1.5 billion package.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I do hope that the Government will stand ready to support Singaporeans should inflation and macroeconomic conditions deteriorate from hereon.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Returning to the proposed amendments to the Stamp Duty Act, I note that this Bill introduces the Additional Conveyance Duties for Trust and the stamp duty treatment for renunciation of interest in residential property that is held on a trust.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: MOF's announcement of the ACD (Trust) follows closely the announcement on the introduction of the ABSD (Trust) on 8 May 2022, which, I recognise, plugs a gap in the existing ABSD and ACD regimes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am reminded of a news article I read in The Business Times late last year, which reported that a certain crypto billionaire – well, at least back then – was at an early stage of buying a S$48.8 million Good Class Bungalow (GCB) as trustee for his nearly three-year-old child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This transaction apparently closed in March this year, but I wonder if headlines, such as this, prompted MOF to undertake a review of the ABSD regime?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, the practice of purchasing residential properties via trusts has been well documented since the implementation of the ABSD regime about a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Not having to pay ABSD for what would have been a multiple property purchase, but with no access to financing were the key features of such purchases, in what some would call a loophole, albeit a well-publicised one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I recognise that this was born out of a periodic policy review, will the Minister shed light on what were the considerations and why is the gap only closed now and not years ago?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What were the number and dollar value of such transactions which have made use of this gap in the ABSD regime, and was there a material increase in such transactions which prompted the MOF review?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That said, I view this development with a glass-half-full lens and it could even be seen as a form of wealth tax which has a targeted and narrow scope.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the introduction of ACD (Trust), as included in the Bill, I recognise that this will go hand in hand with the policy intent of ABSD (Trust), of which I am supportive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am again reminded of news from yesteryears, when ACD itself first came into effect in March 2017.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unbeknownst to many, stamp duties on the transfer of shares in a company are only levied on net asset values, and at a mere 0.2%, significantly lower in rate and tax base, as compared to buyers' stamp duties and ABSD levied on the value of the residential properties themselves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back then, there were several bulk sales of properties by developers via the sale of property holding entities, to avoid extension charges under the qualifying certificate, or QC, conditions for not completing the sale of all residential properties by certain deadlines.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This loophole was, subsequently, closed with the introduction of ACD.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I recognise the policy intent of QC and ABSD in ensuring developers do not hoard inventory, the current ABSD remission rules for developers, in particular, cause greater cyclicality in the residential market, arguably, as it imposes harsh ABSD penalties for failing to complete the sale of all residential units within the prescribed period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would apply, regardless of whether the project has 2,000, 200 or 20 units to begin with, and could even have discouraged developers from triggering for what would have been our first master developer site in Kampong Bugis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As part of its periodic policy review, is MOF looking at reviewing the ABSD remission conditions for property developers to ensure greater stability in the property market?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Stamp duties represent a not insignificant upfront cost for home buyers even in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this may not mean much in percentage terms as compared to the price of the flat, in absolute terms, assuming one saves $500 a month, stamp duties could represent close to 20 months' worth of savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government should have introduced this Bill at least 10 years ago, perhaps around 2011, when the Additional Buyers' Stamp Duty (ABSD) was introduced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And are there any properties being sold to realise a profit while under a living trust without paying the ABSD?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given Singapore already has a tax regime that favours the rich, such tax loopholes are inexcusable and should be dealt with strictly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, we propose two amendments to this new Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will eliminate the trouble of having to determine whether the living trust is genuine or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill to levy stamp duty on living trusts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government should have introduced this Bill at least 10 years ago, around 2011, when the Additional Buyer Stamp Duty (ABSD) was introduced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are disappointed that the Government has allowed loopholes in ABSD to be left open and exploited by some rich buyers of properties for so long.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We ask the Government to tell us the number and value of properties transferred to living trusts since the introduction of ABSD in 2011.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And are there any properties being sold to realise a profit while under a living trust without paying ABSD?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given Singapore already has a tax regime that favours the rich, such tax loopholes are inexcusable and should be dealt with strictly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, we propose two amendments to this new Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will eliminate the trouble of having to determine whether the living trust is genuine or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill and propose that a thorough review of property market policies be conducted by the Government before Singaporeans are further disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill and propose that a more thorough review of the property market policies be conducted by the Government before Singaporeans are further disadvantaged.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I propose to take a break now and I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such trusts are instruments only available to the ultra-high-net-worth individuals who can afford to pay for the properties in cash, it is all the more important that we close the loopholes which may be exploited by such buyers to avoid paying ABSD.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, the introduction of the Additional Conveyance Duties (ACD) for Trust and the stamp duty treatment for renunciation of interest in residential property that is held on a trust, are welcomed, particularly during this period of widening income equality.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I agree with the Ministry that such measures are necessary to promote an equitable and sustainable residential property market, where the high-net-worth individuals should not have a particular advantage in avoiding taxes which other property buyers would have to pay.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Investors may seek to transfer ownership of properties into such trusts to avoid the duties.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since ABSD was introduced in December 2011, the Government has reviewed and raised the rates, to ensure a stable residential property market.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Government has also made refinements, including introducing ACD, to ensure that the policies meet the objectives.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, based on feedback that we hear from time to time, the interest to find ways to avoid such duties will remain and even grow stronger.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What will MOF do to ensure that ABSD and ACD will not be easily avoided?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, may I ask the Minister what is the expected impact on Singapore as a wealth management hub?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would these changes reduce Singapore’s appeal to the ultra-high-net-worth group?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This applies for both pre-existing trusts and new trusts created on or after 9 May 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Living trusts are trusts that come into existence during the lifetime of the person who created it.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Don Wee have asked whether ABSD (Trust) applies where: the transfer of residential property into a living trust took place before 9 May 2022, which is the effective date of ABSD (Trust); and there is a subsequent appointment or distribution of the property to a beneficiary of the trust on or after 9 May 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Before the introduction of ABSD (Trust), transfers of residential property into a trust with an identifiable beneficial owner are subject to ABSD.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the situation is not entirely as what Mr Louis Chua described and certainly not what Mr Leong Mun Wai said in his speech.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: ABSD collected for transfers into trusts where there is an identifiable beneficial owner of the property was not separately tracked before 9 May 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It was instead accounted for according to the profile of the identifiable beneficial owner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we look at the profile of the beneficial identifiable owner to determine what is the ABSD that is due.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I have explained in my Second Reading speech, ABSD would not apply before 9 May 2022 for trusts which do not have an identifiable beneficial owner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is what the proposed changes for ABSD (Trust) and ACD (Trust) seek to address – to ensure that ABSD and ACD continue to remain relevant as property market cooling measures, irrespective of whether trusts are used or not.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Trusts can be set up for different reasons, including for non-tax purposes, such as to provide for charitable giving.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Given the diversity and complexity of trust instruments, we decided to study the proposed changes carefully and do a thorough review, so that we could achieve our policy objectives while avoiding unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I am glad that all the Members who have spoken agree with the proposed changes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will allow us to move forward to apply the new changes with effect from 9 May in the manner which I described earlier.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is important for us to also remember that when we implement some of these changes, we also have to bear in mind how they will fit in with our overall system of governance and rule of law.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also mentioned whether we could refund ABSD only when the creator of the trust or the settler has died, again, if I heard him correctly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we actually collect the full amount upfront and we only refund when certain conditions are met, and you would have to apply.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this, actually, is even better than what Mr Leong Mun Wai mentioned, which is to only refund when the creator or the settler has passed away.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Importantly, Madam, we also have to take a look at what is our overall tax and transfer system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I do not agree with what Mr Leong Mun Wai said that our tax and transfer system benefit the rich.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We did this in Budget 2010, 2013, 2018 and, more recently, in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In Budget 2015 and Budget 2022, we also raised the income tax for higher income earners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, overall, our system of taxes and benefits is a fair and progressive one.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is one where everyone contributes but those who have more will pay more, contribute more than what they receive in terms of benefits.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The associate relationship Mr Louis Ng refers to is part of the current definition of "associates" under the existing ACD regime and it is not an amendment that is being proposed in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I had earlier explained that where a trustee holds equity interests for a beneficiary who is not an identifiable beneficial owner of those interests at the time of their transfer into the trust, such a beneficiary is considered an associate of the trustee in determining whether the trustee is a significant owner of the PHE.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this definition of associates will be provided for in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Today, if ACD is payable, the grantee or grantor is required to stamp the instrument and submit to IRAS a copy of the instrument and supporting documents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These supporting documents include a declaration of associates and the equity interests in the PHE that they beneficially own.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this includes associates who are parties with an oral or implied agreement or arrangement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS will conduct a thorough assessment of the documents submitted, including verifying the existence of any oral or implied agreement or arrangement, using a risk-based approach.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For instance, IRAS may interview the parties involved.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have stringent enforcement in Singapore and there are stiff penalties for tax evasion, whether on stamp duties or other taxes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, for people who are thinking of circumventing the rules, please do not, because there will be a price to pay when you are caught.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Don Wee asked how much more the new stamp duties are expected to contribute to Government revenue.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Chua also alluded to this in his speech.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Don Wee has asked whether the amendments would apply to a trust created overseas.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These amendments are applicable to two groups of instruments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, an instrument executed outside of Singapore, relating to a property situated in Singapore and received in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is regardless of whether the trust is created locally or overseas.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Chua asked whether MOF is reviewing the ABSD remission conditions for housing developers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The three- and five-year deadlines for non-licensed and licensed developers to sell their developments remain relevant to ensure a timely sale of such units to the market instead of keeping them for future sale for possibly higher prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The deadlines also encourage developers to bid for residential land prudently.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The vast majority of developers are able to meet these deadlines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Chua also asked if the Government would consider a move similar to what was done in New South Wales, Australia, to replace the upfront stamp duty with an annual property tax for first-time home buyers who purchase properties below a certain amount.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: According to reports from the New South Wales government, the home ownership rate had declined for each generation since the baby boomers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, 60% of people born between 1942 and 1951 owned homes by age 25 to 34.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This dropped by 15 percentage points to 45% for those born 1982 to 1991.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: About 90% of Singaporean families own their own homes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And there is no ABSD for Singaporeans who are buying their first residential property.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Importantly, we have good quality public housing which caters to the housing needs of the large majority of our first-time buyers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With subsidies and grants and with mortgage financing provided by HDB, our public housing – HDB flats – remains affordable for first-time home buyers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is important for us to bear in mind the differences in our context and our situation when we consider whether we want to adopt ideas and practices from overseas jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Their policies are designed to tackle their challenges, which may not be the same as what we face in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: ABSD or ACD already apply to purchases of residential properties in Singapore or transfers of equity interests in property holding entities, as part of our property market cooling measures.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proposed amendments in this Bill are to ensure a fair and consistent tax treatment when such purchases or transfers are made through trusts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do not expect ABSD (Trust), ACD (Trust) and the imposition of stamp duty on the renunciation of a trust property to affect Singapore's position as a wealth management hub.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I thank the Senior Minister of State for replying to my questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is, my understanding is that, in the past, before 9 May 2022, ABSD is not collected from trusts that do not have identifiable beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If that is the case, if my understanding is right, can I have the number of trusts that have taken advantage of this ABSD loophole?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If the number is available, I would like to have it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State if he has the following characteristics inside the tax system, does he consider it favouring the rich or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Two, low personal income taxes, even at 22% or 24% after the revision this year, after the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The effective income tax is actually lower than that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, if you are very rich, you have an income of $5 million, you may be very close to the 24%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But our sliding income tax structure means that the effective tax rate is actually lower than the highest income tax rate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, generally, our personal income tax is very low.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Fourth, no tax on interest, one layer of tax on dividends only, which is quite extraordinary, compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, with all these, can we still say that our system is one that favours the rich?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But as I have said earlier in my response, I thank Members for their support.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not wish to veer into a separate debate about the tax system in general because this debate today is on the Second Reading of the Stamp Duties (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Those who have less, those who are more vulnerable, the lower-income, they will receive more benefits and more help.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That, to me, is what a fair and just society is about.      .
